scenes.title: Foundation: systems and row operations
scenes.objective: Recall matrix form and elementary row operations.

ask.q: How is a linear system written in matrix form?
ask.nudge: Use A for coefficients, x for unknowns and b for constants.

body: A system of m linear equations in n unknowns can be written Ax=b. The coefficient matrix A and augmented matrix [A|b] contain the information needed for consistency and solution structure.
Gaussian elimination uses elementary row operations to simplify the system without changing its solution set. Pivot positions reveal rank and the number of free variables.

items.recall: A form where non-zero rows are above zero rows and each leading entry moves right as you go down.
refresh: The leading non-zero entry of each non-zero row is a pivot. Rows of zeros, if any, appear at the bottom, and pivot positions move strictly right in successive rows.
Echelon form is enough to read rank and perform back-substitution. Reduced row echelon form goes further by making each pivot one and clearing its column above and below.

items.ask: What is the rank of a matrix?
items.recall: The number of pivots, equivalently the number of non-zero rows in echelon form.
refresh: Rank is the dimension of the row space and column space. Elementary row operations preserve rank, so row reduction is a valid way to calculate it.
For an augmented system, compare rank(A) with rank([A|b]). The extra column may create a new pivot and make the system inconsistent.

items.recall: A variable corresponding to a non-pivot column.
refresh: Each pivot column gives a leading variable. Non-pivot columns correspond to free variables that can be assigned arbitrary values in a consistent system.
If there are n unknowns and rank r, a consistent system has n−r free variables. Thus r=n gives a unique solution, while r<n gives infinitely many solutions.

scenes.title: Consistency is about the augmented column
scenes.objective: Understand why the right-hand side matters.

ask.q: Can Ax=b be inconsistent even when A has full column rank?
ask.nudge: Yes, if b is not in the column space of A.

body: The equation Ax=b is consistent exactly when b belongs to the column space of A. Row reduction detects the failure as a row [0 … 0 | c] with c≠0.
The augmented matrix records the right-hand side. A new pivot in the augmented column increases the rank and signals inconsistency.

scenes.title: Gaussian elimination and RREF
scenes.objective: Recognise echelon and reduced echelon forms.

ask.q: What is the rank of a matrix in row echelon form?
ask.nudge: Count the non-zero rows or pivots.

blocks.body: Swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero scalar, or add a multiple of one row to another. These operations preserve the solution set and rank.
REF has staircase pivots. RREF additionally has leading ones and zeros everywhere else in each pivot column.
Pivot variables are expressed in terms of free variables. If no contradictory row occurs, assign arbitrary values to the free variables and back-substitute.

scenario.teaser: A set of simultaneous balance equations is solved by elimination.
scenario.title: Solving a small balance model
body: A simple resource or accounting model can produce several simultaneous linear equations. Writing them as Ax=b makes the coefficient structure explicit.
Gaussian elimination transforms the augmented matrix into an equivalent system that is easier to solve. Each row operation preserves the solution set.
The pivot pattern then reveals whether the model has one solution, infinitely many solutions or no solution. This structural diagnosis is often more important than the arithmetic alone.

ask.q: What is the consistency criterion for Ax=b?
ask.nudge: Compare the coefficient and augmented ranks.

blocks.body: If consistent and rank(A)=n, the solution is unique. If consistent and rank(A)<n, there are infinitely many solutions.
If rank(A)<rank([A|b]), a contradictory row appears in the reduced augmented matrix, such as 0=non-zero.

scenes.title: Guided: identify inconsistency
scenes.objective: Use an augmented pivot to reject a system.
scenes.problem: A row-reduced augmented matrix contains [0,0,0|5]. Is the system consistent?
hints: No values of the variables can satisfy 0=5.
The augmented rank exceeds the coefficient rank.
scenes.solution: The row [0,0,0|5] represents 0=5, a contradiction. Therefore rank([A|b])>rank(A), and no solution exists.

ask.q: Would the homogeneous system Ax=0 ever be inconsistent?
ask.nudge: The zero vector is always a solution.

ask.q: For an n-unknown homogeneous system with rank r, what is the dimension of its solution space?

blocks.body: Ax=0 is always consistent because x=0 is a solution.
For A with n columns, dim Null(A)=n−rank(A). This is the number of free variables in the reduced system.
A homogeneous system has a non-zero solution iff rank(A)<n. If rank(A)=n, the zero solution is unique.

scenes.title: Guided: count solutions
scenes.objective: Use rank and number of unknowns.
scenes.problem: A consistent system has 5 unknowns and rank 3. How many free variables does it have?
hints: The number of pivot variables equals rank.
Subtract rank from the number of columns.
scenes.solution: The nullity is 5−3=2. Since the system is consistent and has free variables, it has infinitely many solutions.

ask.q: If the system were homogeneous, would it be consistent?
ask.nudge: Yes, the zero vector always solves it.

items.q: When is a consistent solution unique?
items.a: When rank(A)=n, the number of unknowns.

scenes.title: Pivots reveal the geometry of solutions
scenes.objective: Interpret unique, infinite and no-solution cases.

ask.q: What does a free variable mean geometrically?
ask.nudge: The solution set has a direction of freedom.

body: A unique solution is a single point. One free variable typically gives a line of solutions; two free variables typically give a plane, subject to the system being consistent.
An inconsistent system has no point satisfying all equations. The rank comparison distinguishes this from a non-unique but consistent solution set.

scenario.teaser: A model may have redundant equations or incompatible measurements.
scenario.title: Consistency checks in a data-balance system
body: A set of balance equations may contain redundant relationships. Row reduction identifies redundant rows as zero rows and shows how many independent equations remain.
If a measurement or right-hand side conflicts with the coefficient relationships, the augmented matrix gains an extra pivot and the system becomes inconsistent.
This diagnosis separates lack of information (free variables) from contradictory information (no solution). It is a useful first check before interpreting estimated parameters.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.objective: Avoid common rank and consistency errors.
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.why: The zero vector is always a solution.

items.claim: A consistent system with rank below n has a unique solution.
items.why: It has at least one free variable and infinitely many solutions.

items.claim: A row [0 … 0 | c] with c≠0 signals inconsistency.
The number of free variables is n−rank(A).
items.why: This is rank-nullity for the coefficient matrix.

items.claim: Row operations can change the solution set.
items.why: Elementary row operations preserve the solution set.

scenes.title: Final linear-systems checklist
scenes.objective: Use RREF and rank to classify a system.
body: 1. Write Ax=b and form the augmented matrix [A|b].
2. Use elementary row operations to reach echelon form or RREF.
3. Rank(A) is the number of coefficient pivots; rank([A|b]) includes any augmented pivot.
4. Consistent iff the two ranks are equal.
6. Infinitely many iff consistent and rank(A)<n; free variables=n−rank(A).
7. Homogeneous systems are always consistent; non-trivial solutions exist iff rank(A)<n.
